title: Water Treatment Concepts for Operators
audience: Operators, trainees and supervisors who run or support a conventional surface water or groundwater treatment plant and want a clear foundation before a process-control course.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic. Basic Math is helpful but not required. Jurisdiction-neutral: no regulatory limits are stated in this course.
introduction: Build the foundation for a conventional treatment plant: where the raw water comes from, how the treatment train is ordered, what coagulation, flocculation and sedimentation do, how filters and disinfectant residuals work, and which numbers tell an operator that the process is working. Each module has worked scenarios, quick checks that explain the reasoning behind each answer, and a short written assignment. The course gives general principles. Plant-specific limits and procedures come from your own plant and regulator.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Source water and the treatment train
objectives: Describe the main sources of raw water and the quality concerns each usually brings.
Explain the treatment train and why each barrier is placed where it is.
modules.lesson: ### What the plant starts with Every treatment plant begins with water that has not been made safe yet. The raw water quality decides which processes are needed, how much chemical is used and what can go wrong. An operator who knows the source water can predict many problems before they show up on a gauge. Raw water is not one thing. It can be a river that rises after a storm, a lake that turns over in spring, or a well whose quality changes slowly over years. ### Where water comes from Surface water, such as rivers, lakes and reservoirs, carries suspended solids, algae, organic matter and microbes. Its quality can change within hours of a heavy rain. Groundwater usually has lower turbidity and a steadier temperature, but it can carry dissolved iron, manganese, hardness or hydrogen sulfide. Groundwater that is under the influence of surface water can carry the same risks as surface water, so its source must be checked rather than assumed. Source water protection reduces what enters the plant at the start, which is usually cheaper than removing it later. ### The treatment train and multiple barriers A treatment train is the sequence of processes from the intake to the clearwell. A typical surface water train includes screening, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation or flotation, filtration, disinfection and storage. Each step is a barrier that removes or inactivates part of the risk. The multiple-barrier idea means that a weak step is backed up by the next one. A plant should not rely on a single barrier to do the whole job. ### Why the order matters Order matters because each step prepares the water for the next. Coagulation has to come before settling, because settling works poorly on particles that stay dispersed. Filtration removes what settling leaves behind. Disinfection usually comes after particle removal, because particles can shield microbes from the disinfectant. Moving a step changes what every later step has to handle, so an operator who changes one process should ask what it does to the rest of the train. ### What operators watch first Operators watch a small set of numbers that show whether the process is working: raw water turbidity, pH, temperature, chemical dose, filter effluent turbidity and the disinfectant residual at the end of the train. Trends matter more than single readings. Rising raw turbidity with an unchanged dose tells a different story from the same turbidity with a dose that has been raised to match it.

Brookmere is a fictional town whose plant normally draws from a river intake. During a repair to the intake, operators switched part of the supply to a shallow well for ten days. Within a week the raw water colour rose, the coagulant dose had to change, and the filter run times became shorter. List the treatment barriers the water passes through, in order. For the colour change, name the barrier most affected, the measurement you would use to track it, and what you would do if it kept rising. Name any question you could not answer from the scenario.

Watch for learners who call any process a barrier without saying what it removes.

checks.prompt: Which source is most likely to show rapid turbidity changes after heavy rain?
choices: A river intake
A deep confined aquifer well
A sealed bedrock well
A protected spring with a long residence time
checks.explanation: Rivers collect runoff directly, so turbidity can rise within hours of heavy rain. Deep and sealed sources buffer that change.

checks.prompt: Which quality concern is most typical of groundwater?
choices: Large numbers of suspended algae
Dissolved iron and manganese
Storm-driven silt
Oocysts carried in fresh runoff
checks.explanation: Groundwater often carries dissolved metals because minerals dissolve as water moves through the ground. Algae and silt are typical of surface water.

checks.prompt: What does it mean when groundwater is under the influence of surface water?
choices: It is always free of microbes
It is treated exactly like deep groundwater
It can carry surface water risks such as microbes and turbidity spikes
It has no seasonal changes
checks.explanation: Groundwater under the influence of surface water can carry surface risks, so its source must be checked rather than assumed.

checks.prompt: What is the multiple-barrier approach?
choices: Using two chemicals in one tank
Repeating the same filter twice
Testing one sample in two laboratories
Several treatment steps, each able to reduce risk, so one weak step is backed up
checks.explanation: Each step removes or inactivates part of the risk, so a weak step is backed up by the next one.

checks.prompt: Why is coagulation placed before sedimentation?
choices: Coagulation makes small particles clump so they can settle
Sedimentation adds chlorine to the water
Coagulation removes dissolved oxygen
Sedimentation must come before any chemical is added
checks.explanation: Settling works on clumped particles. Coagulation is what makes the small particles clump.

checks.prompt: Why is disinfection usually placed after particle removal?
choices: Particles neutralise chlorine in the pipe
Particles can shield microbes from the disinfectant
Filters need chlorine before they can wash
Disinfectant reacts with the filter media
checks.explanation: Particles can protect microbes from the disinfectant, so removing them first helps disinfection work.

modules.title: Coagulation, flocculation and sedimentation
objectives: Explain why fine particles need a coagulant and what the coagulant does to them.
Relate rapid mixing, flocculation and sedimentation to what the operator sees and measures.
modules.lesson: ### Why particles need help Most particles in raw water are too small and too lightly charged to settle on their own. Their surfaces carry similar electrical charges, so they push each other apart and stay suspended for a very long time. Colour, fine clay and many microbes behave this way. Settling basins and filters cannot remove particles that never clump, so the first job of the coagulation process is to change how those particles behave. ### Rapid mix disperses the coagulant A coagulant is a chemical, such as aluminum sulfate, ferric chloride or a polymer, that neutralises particle charges so the particles can stick together. For this to work, the coagulant must be spread through the whole flow quickly. Rapid mix uses high energy for a short time to do this. If the mixing is weak, the coagulant reacts unevenly, some particles are missed, and the floc that forms later is patchy. ### Flocculation grows the floc After the coagulant has done its work, slower mixing gives the destabilised particles time and chances to collide and join. The result is floc, a cluster of particles large enough to settle. Flocculation mixing has to be gentle enough not to break the floc apart and strong enough to keep the particles in contact. Many plants use stages with less energy in each stage so the growing floc is not sheared apart. ### Sedimentation removes the floc In a sedimentation basin, gravity pulls the floc down to a sludge layer while the clearer water moves on toward the filters. The overflow rate, which is the flow divided by the basin surface area, tells the operator how quickly water is moving through the basin. Short-circuiting happens when water takes a shorter path than the basin was designed for, which lets floc escape to the filters. A sludge blanket of settled solids can also rise and carry floc over the weirs if it is not removed. ### The jar test and what operators watch A jar test runs several beakers of the same water with different coagulant doses, using the same mixing sequence. The operator watches how fast floc forms, how large it gets and how quickly it settles, then checks the turbidity of the supernatant water. The dose that gives good floc and clear water at the lowest practical chemical cost is the starting point for the full plant. Changes in raw water, temperature and pH can change the best dose, so the jar test is repeated when the water changes.

### Fictional scenario: Carrow Creek Water Works

Carrow Creek Water Works is a fictional plant. A spring storm raised raw turbidity from 8 to 40 NTU in one day. The filters began to clog quickly and the settled water turbidity rose. The chief operator asks for a jar test to choose a new alum dose, and the plant's rapid mix has been running at a low setting since a motor repair.

Explain how the weak rapid mix could explain some of the filter problems, and what you would check first. Describes what the jar test compares and the results that choose the dose.

modules.facilitatorGuide: Ask learners to draw the three stages of mixing and say what each one does to the particles. Check that they describe the jar test as a comparison under the same mixing, not a single test. Strong answers link the overflow rate to short-circuiting and carry-over. Watch for learners who say a higher dose always improves settling; a higher dose can restabilise particles and increase sludge.

checks.prompt: Why do fine particles in raw water stay suspended for a long time?
choices: They are too heavy to float
Their surface charges push them apart, so they do not clump
They dissolve in cold water
Sunlight removes them from the surface
checks.explanation: Similar charges repel the particles, so they do not collide and grow into floc.

checks.prompt: What is the main job of a coagulant?
choices: To kill microbes in the water
To raise the pH to neutral
To neutralise particle charges so the particles can clump
To remove dissolved oxygen
checks.explanation: A coagulant reduces the repulsion between particles, which lets them join together.

checks.prompt: Why does rapid mixing use high energy for a short time?
choices: To grow large floc in a single step
To settle particles before flocculation
To remove colour without chemicals
To disperse the coagulant quickly through the water
checks.explanation: Rapid mixing spreads the coagulant evenly before it reacts with the particles.

checks.prompt: What happens if the flocculation mixing is too fast?
choices: Floc can break apart and fail to grow
Floc grows too large to be seen
The coagulant dissolves in the water
Alkalinity rises sharply
checks.explanation: Too much shear breaks the floc, so it cannot grow large enough to settle well.

checks.prompt: What does the overflow rate describe in a sedimentation basin?
choices: The time water spends in the basin only
Flow per unit of basin surface area
The speed of the sludge pump
The number of basins in service
checks.explanation: Overflow rate is flow divided by surface area, so it shows how quickly water rises through the basin.

checks.prompt: What does a jar test help an operator decide?
choices: The age of the filter media
The pipe material in the distribution system
A coagulant dose that gives good floc and clear settled water
The number of operators on shift
checks.explanation: The jar test compares doses under the same mixing and shows which dose gives good floc and clear water.

modules.title: Filtration and disinfection basics
objectives: Explain how granular filters remove particles and how head loss and breakthrough show a filter's condition.
Explain how a disinfectant residual and contact time work together, and where the residual is checked.
modules.lesson: ### What a filter removes Filtration removes the particles and floc that settling leaves behind, along with many microbes that are attached to them. Granular filters are depth filters. The water passes through a bed of media several feet deep, and the particles are trapped throughout the bed, not only on the surface. This is why a filter can hold a large load of solids before it needs cleaning. ### Granular media and depth filtration Many filters use dual or mixed media. Coarser anthracite sits above finer sand, so the water meets larger grains first and then finer ones. This layering lets the filter hold solids through its depth. The media size, depth and loading rate are set by the design, and the operator's job is to keep the bed in the condition the design expects. ### Head loss, run length and breakthrough As particles collect in the media, the pressure drop across the filter rises. This is head loss. Head loss tells the operator how loaded the filter is. Breakthrough happens when particles start to pass through the bed and the filter effluent turbidity rises. A filter that reaches breakthrough before it reaches its planned head loss may have a problem with coagulation, media condition or flow. ### Backwash and filter restart Backwash reverses the flow through the filter so that the media expands and the trapped solids are flushed out to waste. After a backwash, the first water can still carry solids and backwash residue, so many plants run the filter to waste for a set period before returning it to service. The restart is part of the process, not a formality. Turbidity after restart is a sign of whether the filter is ready. ### Disinfection after filtration Disinfection inactivates microbes that remain after treatment. Free chlorine is the chlorine that remains available as hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite after it has reacted with the demand in the water. Demand comes from organic matter, iron, manganese and ammonia. The residual that is left at the end of contact is what protects the distribution system. Contact time matters because the disinfectant needs time with the microbes. The combination of residual and contact time is often described as CT. Clearwell storage and baffling give the contact time that the residual needs, and the residual is checked at the end of the train as well as in the distribution system.

checks.prompt: What does granular media filtration mainly remove?
choices: Dissolved hardness minerals
Dissolved oxygen
Particles and floc that pass the sedimentation step
Free chlorine residual
checks.explanation: Granular filters trap the particles and floc left after settling, along with many attached microbes.

checks.prompt: What is head loss in a filter?
choices: The speed of the backwash pump
The chlorine demand of the water
The temperature of the filter influent
The pressure drop across the filter as particles collect in the media
checks.explanation: Head loss rises as the media collects solids, so it shows how loaded the filter is.

checks.prompt: What is breakthrough?
choices: Particles pass through the media and filter effluent turbidity rises
A cracked filter underdrain
A completed backwash
A chlorine residual that falls to zero
checks.explanation: Breakthrough is when particles get through the bed, which shows up as higher effluent turbidity.

checks.prompt: What does a backwash do?
choices: Adds coagulant to the filter
Expands the media and flushes trapped solids out to waste
Raises the pH of the filter
Removes dissolved minerals
checks.explanation: Backwash reverses the flow so the media expands and the trapped solids leave the filter.

checks.prompt: What is a free chlorine residual?
choices: Chlorine bound only to ammonia
Chlorine that has settled as sludge
Chlorine that remains as hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite after reacting with demand
Chlorine held in the gas cylinder
checks.explanation: The free residual is what is left available to disinfect after the demand has been satisfied.

checks.prompt: Why is contact time important in disinfection?
choices: Contact time increases turbidity
Contact time sets the filter run length
Contact time replaces the need for a residual
The disinfectant needs time in contact with microbes to inactivate them
checks.explanation: Inactivation depends on residual and time together, so a short contact time reduces disinfection.

modules.title: Monitoring, records and troubleshooting
objectives: Choose a monitoring set for a conventional plant and read its trends.
Keep records that can be trusted and escalate a suspected process failure with the evidence.
modules.lesson: ### The numbers that tell the story A conventional plant produces many numbers, but a few carry most of the information. Raw water turbidity and temperature show what the process has to handle. The coagulant dose and pH show what has been done to the water. Filter effluent turbidity shows whether the barriers are working, and the disinfectant residual at the end of the train shows what is left to protect the distribution system. An operator who watches these few numbers every shift can see most changes early. ### Trends beat single readings A single reading is a snapshot. A trend shows the direction and speed of change, which a snapshot cannot. A filter turbidity that is 0.2 NTU higher than yesterday may be normal. The same turbidity rising for six hours is not. Control charts plot results over time against set limits, so an operator can see a shift before a limit is crossed. Trend reading also explains why a stable dose can stop working: the raw water changed and the dose did not follow. ### Records that can be trusted A record is trusted when it is complete, dated, attributed to the operator and kept with the reading it describes. Corrections are made by a single line through the original entry, with the reason, initials and date, so the original stays visible. A record written from memory at the end of a week, or a value changed to match an expected result, is not evidence of what happened. A trustworthy record is also the first thing that a supervisor or auditor will ask to see. ### Troubleshooting from symptom to cause Troubleshooting starts with the symptom and works back. A rising raw turbidity with an unchanged dose may mean the dose no longer matches the water, so the jar test is the next check. Sedimentation problems often show up downstream as rising filter loading or floc in the filter effluent. Short filter runs with good effluent turbidity point to head loss, backwash effectiveness or the raw water load rather than to the disinfectant. A falling residual with long water age often reflects low demand and time in storage. ### When to escalate Escalate when the readings suggest a barrier is not working, not only after a complaint or an equipment failure. A good escalation has three parts: the trend with its readings and times, the actions already taken and their results, and what the operator needs from the supervisor. A sustained shift that the operator cannot explain is a reason to escalate, not a reason to wait for it to correct itself.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional scenario: Northfield Plant's six-hour shift

Northfield Plant is a fictional conventional plant. During one shift, raw turbidity climbed steadily, the alum dose stayed at its setpoint, and filter 3 effluent turbidity drifted from 0.06 to 0.14 NTU. The clearwell residual dropped by 0.2 mg/L. The operator has recorded each reading but has not yet written a note about the trend.
modules.assignment: Prepare an escalation note for Northfield's supervisor. Show the trend in raw turbidity and filter 3 effluent turbidity with their times. State which barrier is most likely affected and why. Describe the actions you would take now, what you would check next and what you need from the supervisor. Correct one record line in the note to show the correction practice.
rubric: Presents the trends with readings and times, not a single reading.
Identifies the barrier most likely affected and gives the reason.
States the actions taken, the checks next and the support needed.
Shows a correction made in the trusted-record way.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Ask learners to say what a control chart adds that a single reading does not. Check that they link the filter effluent drift to a barrier and not only to the disinfectant. Good escalation notes are short and specific, and include what has already been done. Watch for learners who correct a record by erasing it, or who wait for a trend to correct itself.

checks.prompt: Why do operators track trends rather than single readings?
choices: A single reading is always wrong
Trends replace calibration of the instruments
Trends set the price of the chemicals
A trend shows the direction and speed of change, which a single reading cannot
checks.explanation: A trend shows whether a value is rising, falling or steady, which a single reading cannot show.

checks.prompt: Which measurement is a direct check on filter performance?
choices: Filter effluent turbidity
Clearwell temperature
Raw water hardness
Chemical storage level
checks.explanation: Filter effluent turbidity shows how much particulate matter is getting through the filter.

checks.prompt: What makes a plant record trustworthy?
choices: It is written from memory at the end of the week
It is complete, dated, attributed to the operator and kept with the reading
It is changed to match the expected result
It is kept on a scrap sheet
checks.explanation: A trusted record shows what was measured, when, by whom, and it is not changed to fit expectations.

checks.prompt: Raw turbidity rises while the coagulant dose stays the same. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The filters have gone out of service
The chlorine residual has failed
The dose may no longer match the water, so a jar test is the next check
The pump has lost its prime
checks.explanation: A changed raw water quality can mean the existing dose is no longer right, which a jar test can check.

checks.prompt: Which symptom most suggests a problem in the sedimentation basin?
choices: A drop in clearwell pressure
A higher alarm in the chlorine room
Rising raw water temperature alone
Floc carried over to the filters, seen as rising filter loading
checks.explanation: Floc that escapes the basin reaches the filters and shows up as faster loading and higher effluent turbidity.

checks.prompt: When should an operator escalate a suspected process failure?
choices: As soon as the readings suggest a barrier is not working, with the trend and actions taken
After the end of the shift
Only after a customer complaint
Only if the equipment has to be shut down
checks.explanation: Early escalation with the evidence lets the supervisor act before the problem reaches the distribution system.

finalAssessment.prompt: A plant draws from a river. Which change is most likely after several days of heavy rain?
choices: Turbidity and colour rise
Hardness falls to zero
Water temperature rises sharply
Dissolved oxygen becomes unmeasurable
finalAssessment.explanation: Runoff carries sediment and organic colour into the river, so turbidity and colour rise together.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which quality issue is most typical of a deep well?
choices: Cryptosporidium carried by storm runoff
Hardness and dissolved iron
High turbidity from algal growth
Visible silt after a storm
finalAssessment.explanation: Deep wells often carry dissolved minerals such as hardness and iron, and these do not come from storm runoff.

finalAssessment.prompt: Why is source water protection valuable?
choices: It removes the need for any treatment at the plant, so filters and disinfection can be retired
It replaces the disinfection step, so no residual is needed anywhere downstream of the plant
It reduces what enters the plant, which is usually cheaper than removing it later
It makes filters unnecessary because the water arrives already clear and safe to drink
finalAssessment.explanation: Keeping contaminants out of the source costs less than removing them later, but it does not replace treatment.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a conventional surface water train, what usually comes directly after sedimentation?
choices: Raw water intake
Chemical storage
Clearwell storage
Filtration
finalAssessment.explanation: Sedimentation removes most settleable floc, and filtration removes the remaining particles before disinfection.

finalAssessment.prompt: Why does the order of steps in a train matter?
choices: Each step prepares the water for the next, so a wrong order shifts the load
Order only affects the cost of the chemicals used along the train
Order is set only by the pipe material used at the intake and the clearwell outlet
Order has no effect on later steps, because each step works on its own water
finalAssessment.explanation: Each step changes what the next step receives, so moving a step changes the whole train.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which coagulant is commonly used at operator level to remove particles?
choices: Sodium chloride, the common table salt used for brine
Aluminum sulfate (alum)
Sodium bicarbonate, often used to raise alkalinity
Activated carbon, used mainly for taste and odour
finalAssessment.explanation: Alum is a common coagulant. The other choices are not used mainly to make particles clump.

finalAssessment.prompt: Why does alkalinity matter when alum is dosed?
choices: Alkalinity adds free chlorine to the water, which changes the disinfectant demand of the plant
Alkalinity has no effect on coagulation, because alum does not react with the water chemistry
Alum consumes alkalinity, so low alkalinity can drop the pH outside the effective range
High alkalinity can prevent floc from forming in the rapid mix and the flocculation stages
finalAssessment.explanation: Alum uses up alkalinity as it reacts, and the pH can fall outside the range where coagulation works well.

finalAssessment.prompt: A plant's rapid mix is too weak. What is the most likely result?
choices: Floc becomes too large to settle and carries over into the filters
Filter head loss drops because less solids reach the media at all
Disinfectant demand falls because the coagulant has been used up
The coagulant is poorly dispersed, so coagulation is uneven
finalAssessment.explanation: Weak mixing leaves the coagulant unevenly spread, so some particles are missed and the floc is patchy.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which description best matches the purpose of flocculation?
choices: Gentle mixing that lets small particles join into larger floc
High-energy mixing that disperses the chemical through the water quickly
Chlorine addition to kill microbes before the water reaches the filters
Pumping the water up to the clearwell for storage and later use
finalAssessment.explanation: Flocculation is slow, gentle mixing that gives destabilised particles time to collide and grow.

finalAssessment.prompt: A settling basin has short-circuiting. What does that mean?
choices: Sludge is removed too slowly from the bottom of the basin for the design
Water takes a shorter path through the basin than designed
The basin has two outlet pumps running at the same time for the flow
The chemical feed runs continuously at a constant rate through the day
finalAssessment.explanation: Short-circuiting lets water and floc bypass most of the basin, which can carry floc on to the filters.

finalAssessment.prompt: A filter's effluent turbidity rises steadily and its head loss is high. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The clearwell level is too high, so the filter cannot drain to its design level
The disinfectant residual is too high and is blocking flow through the media bed
The media is loaded with solids and the filter is near the end of its run
The backwash pump is oversized for the filter and draws in air during the run
finalAssessment.explanation: High head loss with rising effluent turbidity points to a loaded bed approaching breakthrough.

finalAssessment.prompt: Why is a filter run to waste after backwash?
choices: To add chlorine to the media so that the bed is disinfected before normal service begins
To raise the head loss so that the filter run length can be measured accurately against the design
To test the backwash pump motor and confirm that it can run at the full design flow for a long period
To discard water that may still carry backwash solids before normal service resumes
finalAssessment.explanation: The first water after backwash can carry residual solids, so it is wasted until the filter is ready.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which arrangement describes a dual-media filter in which the grain size changes with depth?
choices: Coarser anthracite on top of finer sand
Finer sand on top of coarser gravel in a layered bed of uniform depth
A single layer of fine clay placed over a bed of coarse stone and gravel
Gravel only with no media, so the water flows straight through the underdrain
finalAssessment.explanation: Dual-media beds place coarser anthracite above finer sand, so the water meets larger grains first.

finalAssessment.prompt: A clearwell's free residual falls sharply in summer. Which factor most likely contributed?
choices: Lower temperature increased the residual and so reduced the water age in the tank
Higher temperature and longer water age increased chlorine demand and decay
The clearwell depth decreased, so the contact time per litre became much shorter
Filter runs got shorter, so more particles reached the clearwell and the chlorine demand fell
finalAssessment.explanation: Warm water and longer water age speed chlorine decay, so the residual falls faster.

finalAssessment.prompt: What is CT in simple terms?
choices: The toxicity of chlorine to people, measured in the lab at the outlet
A count of the tanks and basins that are in service at one time
A product of disinfectant concentration and contact time
The time between backwashes, measured in hours on the filter log
finalAssessment.explanation: CT combines the disinfectant concentration with the contact time it gets, which is why both matter.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which set of measurements best describes a useful monitoring set for a conventional plant?
choices: Only the clearwell level, read once a day, which tells the operator nothing else about the process
Customer complaints alone, collected through the billing system each month and reviewed at year end
Chemical invoice amounts, reviewed each month by the finance office and the purchasing team
Raw turbidity, pH, coagulant dose, filter effluent turbidity and end-of-train residual
finalAssessment.explanation: This set covers the raw water, the chemical treatment, the filter performance and the disinfection outcome.

finalAssessment.prompt: A pH trend falls steadily after alum dosing. What should the operator consider?
choices: Alkalinity may be used up, so the pH may move outside the coagulation range
The filters are plugging with solids, so the head loss rises and the run length falls quickly
The chlorine residual will rise steadily as the pH falls below neutral in the clearwell
The sludge pump is running too fast for the basin's sludge blanket depth and volume
finalAssessment.explanation: Alum consumes alkalinity, so a falling pH can mean coagulation is moving out of its effective range.

finalAssessment.prompt: A reading was entered wrong. What is the correct record practice?
choices: Erase the entry carefully and write the right value in the same space on the sheet so it looks clean
Correct it with a single line, the reason, initials and date, keeping the original visible
Delete the whole sheet and rewrite the entire page from the start of the shift record in neat handwriting
Enter the right value on another sheet only and leave the wrong entry standing on the original sheet
finalAssessment.explanation: The original stays visible and the correction is traceable, which is the standard for a trusted record.

finalAssessment.prompt: A filter's effluent turbidity is acceptable but its run is short. What should be checked?
choices: The clearwell chlorine residual only, because disinfection controls the filter run length
Customer billing data for the month, since complaints can shorten filter runs
The head loss pattern, backwash effectiveness and the raw water load
The chemical delivery schedule and the supplier's price list for the coming quarter
finalAssessment.explanation: Short runs with good effluent point to head loss, backwash and load, not to disinfection or billing.

finalAssessment.prompt: A trend shows a sustained shift that the operator cannot explain. What is the best next step?
choices: Wait a week and see whether the trend corrects itself before taking any action at all
Change the monitoring frequency so that the trend is less visible in the daily summary
Average the readings over the whole shift, drop the outliers and move on to the next task on the list
Record the trend and actions taken, then escalate to the supervisor with the data
finalAssessment.explanation: A sustained unexplained shift needs escalation with the evidence, not delay or a change that hides the trend.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which source is least likely to show rapid turbidity changes?
choices: A shallow river intake
A lake after spring turnover
A deep, protected aquifer
A reservoir after storm inflow
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A deep, protected aquifer buffers the surface changes that drive turbidity in the other sources.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which description best matches surface water?
choices: Water sealed from the surface with a steady temperature and no change from season to season
Water that carries no organic matter and so never needs coagulation or filtration
Water that is always hard and clear, with no change in quality through the year
Water exposed to air and runoff, with quality that can change quickly
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Surface water is exposed to runoff and air, so its quality can change quickly.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What is the main advantage of a well compared with a river intake?
choices: It often has lower turbidity
It contains no dissolved minerals
It does not change with the seasons
It requires no disinfection
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Wells are often filtered by the ground, so they usually have lower turbidity. They can still carry minerals and microbes.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which steps together remove most suspended particles before filtration?
choices: Disinfection with free chlorine applied at the end of the train
Coagulation followed by sedimentation
Clearwell storage of finished water in the reservoir
Fluoridation of the finished water after the clearwell
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Coagulation makes particles clump and sedimentation removes the clumps, so most particles are gone before filtration.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which step usually comes last in a surface water train before the clearwell?
choices: Screening
Coagulation
Disinfection
Source intake
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Disinfection is usually applied after filtration, just before water goes into storage.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which pair describes a common coagulant and its family?
choices: Chlorine gas and a disinfectant
Activated carbon and an adsorbent
Sodium fluoride and a fluoridation agent
Ferric chloride and an iron salt
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Ferric chloride is an iron salt used as a coagulant. The other pairs are not coagulants.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What does a sweep-floc mechanism rely on?
choices: Metal hydroxide precipitates that trap particles as they form
Chlorine that binds directly to the particles and makes them sink to the bottom
Ultraviolet light breaking particles apart so they settle more quickly in the basin
Filters that catch the clumps before they reach the sedimentation basin at all
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: In sweep floc, the precipitates form a web that traps particles as they settle out.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What is a typical result of too much coagulant?
choices: Lower sludge production because the particles are removed before they settle
Poor settling, restabilised particles, and more sludge
Faster settling as a rule, because the floc becomes heavier and denser in the basin
Less need for filtration, since the basin removes almost everything in one step
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Excess coagulant can restabilise particles and add sludge, so settling can get worse.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Why are tapered flocculation stages used in some plants?
choices: To increase the chlorine residual in the water as it moves through the stages
To heat the water so that the coagulant dissolves more readily in the basin
To reduce mixing energy as floc grows, so it is not broken
To remove taste and odour compounds before the water reaches the sedimentation basin
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Tapered stages lower the mixing energy as the floc gets bigger, which protects the floc from breaking.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What does a sludge blanket indicate in a clarifier?
choices: A layer of oil that floats on the surface of the basin and must be skimmed off
The depth of the filter media in the filter beds, measured from the top surface
A layer of chlorine gas that rises from the basin's outlet channel and weir
A layer of settled solids that water passes through
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A sludge blanket is a layer of settled solids. If it rises too high, floc can be carried over the weirs.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which media is commonly used in a granular filter?
choices: Anthracite and sand
Clay tiles
Stainless steel mesh
Ion-exchange beads
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Anthracite and sand are common granular media. The other items are not filter media in a typical plant.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What is the main purpose of a filter's underdrain?
choices: To add chemicals to the water as it passes through the filter media bed
To collect filtered water and support the media evenly
To measure the turbidity of the water leaving the filter at the outlet
To dewater the sludge so that it can be hauled away as a solid cake
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The underdrain collects filtered water and supports the media, and it also distributes the backwash flow.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Why do operators watch the turbidity of each filter?
choices: To set the chlorine dose for the whole plant and the clearwell at once
To set the sludge removal rate on the sedimentation basin for each shift
To detect breakthrough and check filter performance
To determine the pump speed for the high-service pumps at the outlet
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Filter turbidity is the direct check that the filter is removing particles and that breakthrough has not started.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What is chlorine demand?
choices: The chlorine already present in the supply as a residual in the distribution system
The chlorine stored in the pipes of the distribution system during low demand
The feed rate of the chlorine pump, measured in pounds per day at the feed point
The chlorine used up by reactions before a residual remains
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Demand is the chlorine that is consumed by reactions, so it has to be supplied before a residual can form.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Why is the residual measured at the end of the train?
choices: It shows how much disinfection capacity reaches the distribution system
It shows the filter run time and the head loss pattern across the filter bed
It sets the coagulant dose used in the rapid mix and the flocculation stages
It replaces turbidity monitoring at the filter outlet so that turbidity is not needed
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The end-of-train residual shows what is left to protect the water as it moves into the system.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Why measure raw water temperature?
choices: It sets the chlorine demand directly, so the residual can be read from it
It affects coagulation and settling and can change the best dose
It determines the filter media size needed for the design flow rate
It replaces pH measurement, since temperature gives the same information
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Temperature changes how coagulation and settling behave, which can change the dose that works best.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What does a control chart show?
choices: The price of the chemicals used at the plant over the past twelve months
The layout of the plant, with each process and piece of equipment labelled
Results over time against set limits, showing trends and shifts
The age and training history of the operators on each shift at the plant
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A control chart plots results over time so that trends and shifts show before a limit is crossed.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What should a shift log include?
choices: Only the weather conditions for the shift, recorded at the start of each day
Only the final readings taken just before the shift handover to the next operator
Only the names of the customers who called the plant during the shift
Events, readings, actions taken and the operator's name
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A useful shift log records what happened, what was measured, what was done and who did it.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: The clearwell residual falls and the water age is high. What is a likely cause?
choices: Low demand and long residence time let the residual decay
High demand and short residence time, which keeps the water fresh in the tank
Low temperature and high demand, which slows the decay of the residual in the tank
A blocked filter underdrain that stops filtered water reaching the clearwell
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Long residence time at low demand gives the residual time to decay, so the residual falls.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which information makes an escalation most useful?
choices: A general feeling that something is wrong with the process at the plant
The readings, the trend, what has already been done and what is needed
Only the name of the equipment involved and the make of its control panel
A request for a meeting next week to discuss the problem with the team
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A useful escalation gives the evidence, the actions already taken and the support needed.
